newsitem.title: FALKLAND ISLANDS: Lone U.S. yachtswoman rescued off Falklands.
newsitem.headline: Lone U.S. yachtswoman rescued off Falklands.

text.p: A lone American round-the-world yachtswoman was rescued by Britain's Royal Navy on Monday after she suffered a suspected heart attack in the South Atlantic off the Falklands Islands.
Karen Thorndyke, 52, from Seattle, Washington, in her 36-foot sloop Amelia, was aiming to become the first American woman to sail single-handed around the world.
British forces in the Falklands received a distress call on Sunday night and early on Monday morning Thorndyke was taken aboard the frigate HMS Norfolk, officials said.
A statement from Royal Navy Fleet Headquarters at Northwood, near London, said: "The Amelia was found about 350 miles north of the Falkland Islands in strong winds and rough seas."
She had notified her control, John Oman in Seattle, that she feared she had suffered a heart attack, the navy said.
The frigate's doctor, Surgeon Lieutenant Fleur Marshall, decided that Thorndyke was in fact suffering from an acute angina attack.
Thorndyke will be taken to hospital in the Falklands capital Port Stanley when the Norfolk reaches the south Atlantic islands on Tuesday.
Her yacht, named after the famous flyer Amelia Earhart, was being sailed back to the Falkands by four members of the Norfolk's crew and was not expected to arrive before Friday.
Since beginning her round-the-world effort in October 1995, Thorndyke has been forced to return to San Diego twice -- once from Oregon and once from Nicaragua -- for repairs to her yacht.
She said that she had "sold everything I owned to enable me to buy the yacht".
She rounded Cape Horn just after New Year and spent several weeks in the Falklands before setting off for Australia from Port Stanley last Wednesday.
